title: Sebastian and the Parish
premise: When insurance investigator Rosalind Nakamura is handed the cold case of Marion Voss—a parish organist who vanished fifteen years ago—she expects a routine file. Instead, the recovered diary contains entries written after the disappearance, in handwriting that matches her own. As Rosalind digs into the close-knit congregation of St. Alder's Parish, she uncovers a thirty-year-old cover-up binding the town's most beloved families, and begins to suspect her own memory has been edited—by someone who knew exactly how it works. The trail leads to Father Ambrose, the dying priest who raised her after her parents' death, and to the truth that she and Marion were both witnesses to the same crime as children. In the end, Rosalind must choose between protecting the found family that lied to keep her safe and exposing the truth that will shatter the parish—and herself.
about_author: Sable Crane is the pen name of a former small-town court reporter who spent a decade transcribing other people's secrets before writing them down instead. They live somewhere with too much rain and write mysteries about towns that remember too little.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She takes the Voss file as a favor to the sheriff, cataloguing St. Alder's Parish with her trademark precision: alibis, hymn schedules, funeral rosters. A detail snags—Marion's diary was found open to a page dated three days after she vanished. Emotional beat: quiet unease beneath professional calm.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Forensic analysis confirms the post-disappearance diary entries are authentic—and the final entry describes watching someone from the choir loft, someone 'who remembers everything.' Rosalind realizes the description fits her. Emotional beat: the investigator becomes the investigated.

chapters.title: The Choir Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Deacon Hollis, the parish's loyal fixer. He quietly warns old congregants that an insurance woman is asking questions. Flashback threads reveal the night of Marion's disappearance through his fractured memory. Emotional beat: loyalty curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She maps the parish's interlocking alibis for two separate nights—Marion's disappearance and, thirty years earlier, a fire in the rectory nursery. The same five names appear on both lists. Emotional beat: the thrill of pattern recognition turning to dread.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Forgot
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Her photographic memory fails her for the first time: images of her childhood at the parish are vivid but subtly wrong—a window facing the wrong way, a fourth chair at a table of three. Someone taught her false memories. Emotional beat: grief for a self she can't trust.

chapters.title: The Dying Confessor
chapters.summary: Father Ambrose's POV. The priest, fading in hospice, recalls taking in orphaned Rosalind and sealing away what she witnessed in the nursery fire. He wrote to Marion years ago; her reply said she'd come back to finish it. Emotional beat: love weaponized as protection, guilt without absolution.

chapters.title: Someone Is Filing Me
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Her apartment is searched—not robbed, curated. Files rearranged alphabetically, her way, by someone who knows her methods intimately. She finds a duplicate diary page in her own handwriting she never wrote. Emotional beat: paranoia sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Night of the Nursery Fire
chapters.summary: Deacon Hollis's POV. The full truth surfaces: the fire covered the death of the bishop's illegitimate child; child-Rosalind saw it, and Marion, the young organist, hid her and fled rather than let the parish silence them both. Marion didn't vanish—she was exiled and kept silent by threat. Emotional beat: horror at how deep protection's rot goes.

chapters.title: Vespers
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, climax. Lured to evening service by a forged note in Marion's hand, Rosalind confronts the last living conspirator—the bishop's widow, who has watched Rosalind for fifteen years and edited her memories to keep the parish's peace. A standoff in the choir loft; Hollis breaks ranks and testifies. Emotional beat: truth offered like a blade or a key.

chapters.title: A New Index
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, resolution. The widow confesses; Ambrose dies having heard Rosalind forgive him without excusing him. Marion, alive under another name, sends one final diary entry—addressed to Rosalind this time. Rosalind closes the Voss file and opens a blank notebook. Emotional beat: identity rebuilt not from recovered memory, but chosen truth.
